Generative Cinematographer:
Composing Camera and Object Motion in 3D

Jiahan Zhang    Chaohao Yang    Namitha Guruprasad    Vivekjyoti Banerjee Affiliation: Trong-Tung Nguyen    Alan Yuille    Anand Bhattad Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University
Abstract

Current controllable video generation systems often rely on 2D motion trajectories or sparse drag signals for object motion. These controls are ambiguous because the same 2D trajectory can correspond to different 3D motions, especially when the camera and objects move simultaneously. We present Generative Cinematographer (GenCine), a system that lifts a single image into an editable 3D scene scaffold where artists jointly author camera and foreground motion. Artists specify a camera path and move selected foreground regions using local 3D motion handles. Several handles can move different parts of a subject independently, providing a piecewise-rigid approximation to non-rigid motion without a physics simulator or category-specific prior. To communicate these controls to a pretrained video model, we project them into guidance maps. These maps record where the controlled regions appear in each frame, assign each handle a fixed color across frames and encode the current 3D positions of its controlled points in the same world coordinate system as the background. This lets us describe object motion relative to the scene even as the camera moves. For training, we recover controls from the motion observed in real videos and use ground-truth geometry and trajectories from synthetic videos. We train a lightweight guidance branch and LoRA adapters on a pretrained Wan model to follow these controls. Our experiments show consistent camera-relative motion, improved geometric consistency under viewpoint changes, and strong controllability across diverse real-world scenes.

Project Website: https://generative-cinematographer.github.io/

1 Introduction

“Just as one can compose colors, or forms, so one can compose motions.”
— Alexander Calder (1933)

Composing a cinematic shot means deciding how the camera and the subjects move together. Classical graphics systems such as the Virtual Cinematographer (He et al., 1996) compose shots by controlling a camera within a modeled 3D scene. We bring this world-space approach to video generation, allowing artists to jointly author camera and object motion using a 3D scaffold lifted from a single image (Fig. 1). Generative video models can now synthesize plausible motion from a single image, but giving artists precise control over these movements remains difficult. Text prompts can describe an action but leave its precise path unspecified. Likewise, a 2D drag may correspond to several 3D motions or mix object movement with a change in viewpoint (Fig. 2). A generated video can therefore look plausible while following a different motion from the one the artist intended.

Many controllable video methods specify foreground motion through pixel displacements (Wu et al., 2024; Geng et al., 2024), leaving the underlying 3D motion implicit. Physics simulators and category-specific priors provide additional structure (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b), but their applicability depends on the materials and objects they support. Learning 3D control from videos presents a further challenge: reliable 3D motion annotations are scarce. Synthetic data provide these annotations but differ visually from real footage, while per-pixel 2D conditioning (Chu et al., 2025) leaves artists working in image space.

A natural way to express the intended motion is to place the camera and subjects in a shared 3D scene. Camera paths then describe how the viewpoint changes, while object trajectories describe how the scene itself changes. We follow this approach in Generative Cinematographer (GenCine). Starting from a single image, we lift the scene into a colored point cloud. The artist selects a few foreground regions and specifies how each should move in 3D, along with a camera path. Each selected region acts as a motion handle: its points move together as a rigid group. Several handles can move different parts of a subject independently, providing a piecewise-rigid approximation to non-rigid motion without a skeleton, physics simulator, or category-specific prior.

To train the model, we recover examples of the motion an artist might specify. For real videos, 3D foundation models estimate geometry and camera motion. We use these estimates to lift tracked foreground points into 3D, group nearby tracks into local handles, and use their observed motion as approximate 3D controls. Synthetic videos supply ground-truth geometry and trajectories. Each clip is thus paired with controls describing the motion that actually occurs in it; its first frame supplies the reference image, and the clip supplies the target video.

A pretrained video model does not directly interpret a camera path or a collection of 3D point trajectories. We need a representation that fits its image-based input while retaining what the controls mean. Recent methods support joint camera and object control (Zheng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a); VerseCrafter, for example, uses RGB and depth maps of a background point cloud and object-level Gaussian trajectories. Our representation separates three questions: where does a region appear, which region is it, and how does it move in the world? First, we view the scene through the specified camera at each frame, placing guidance at the projected locations of background and handle points. Second, a fixed color identifies each handle across frames. Third, separate colors encode the current 3D positions of foreground points and the fixed positions of background points. These form the foreground identity, foreground XYZ, and background XYZ maps. The two XYZ maps use the same world frame and scale: camera motion changes where a static point appears, whereas object motion also changes its world position. This distinction preserves information that a 2D trajectory alone discards.

We construct these guidance sequences for each training clip and encode them with the pretrained video model’s frozen video autoencoder. The diffusion model learns to generate the paired video from its first frame, text, and encoded guidance. We train a lightweight side branch and LoRA adapters while keeping the base model weights frozen, allowing the model to learn control without retraining its visual prior. At inference, an artist’s camera path and handle trajectories pass through the same map construction in place of recovered motion. Varying the number and placement of training handles exposes the model to the sparse, partial controls available during authoring.

Our contributions are: (1) a visual guidance representation for 3D motion that preserves handle identity and foreground–background positions in a shared world frame while remaining compatible with pretrained video models; (2) a local 3D motion-handle formulation that approximates non-rigid motion through independently controlled local rigid regions, without requiring a simulator or category-specific prior; and (3) a shared training and authoring pipeline that learns from videos paired with 3D motion controls and generates videos from a single image using artist-authored camera paths and local object trajectories.

2 Related Work

Virtual cinematography.

The graphics community has long studied camera motion authoring. The Virtual Cinematographer (He et al., 1996) formalized shot composition as cinematographic idioms. Later work extended this to declarative camera planning (Christianson et al., 1996) and procedural camera control (Drucker et al., 1992). These systems assume a fully modeled 3D scene. In contrast, GenCine uses a 3D scaffold lifted from a single image to control the video generator.

Camera and motion control in video diffusion.

MotionCtrl (Wang et al., 2024) and CameraCtrl (He et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025b) condition generation on camera poses. GEN3C (Ren et al., 2025) renders a depth-derived 3D cache under target poses, while DimensionX (Sun et al., 2025) generates 3D and 4D scenes from one image. WorldReel (Fang et al., 2025) jointly generates RGB frames, point maps, camera trajectories, and flow for geometric and motion consistency. Generative Camera Dolly (Van Hoorick et al., 2024), TrajectoryCrafter (Yu et al., 2025), and FreeOrbit4D (Cao et al., 2026) redirect viewpoints in existing videos, with FreeOrbit4D reconstructing a geometry-complete 4D proxy. Vista4D (Lin et al., 2026) reshoots source videos using rendered 4D point clouds with temporally persistent static points. MotionCtrl also supports object control; CineMaster (Wang et al., 2025c) uses 3D box layouts, and Diffusion as Shader (Gu et al., 2025) uses 3D tracking videos for joint control.

Object motion control.

DragNUWA (Yin et al., 2023), DragAnything (Wu et al., 2024), and ATI (Wang et al., 2025a) control motion through image-space trajectories; other methods use entities (Wan et al., 2024) or masks and boxes (Li et al., 2025a). Motion-I2V (Shi et al., 2024) predicts motion before synthesis, while Wan-Move (Chu et al., 2025) propagates latent features along trajectories. Motion Prompting (Geng et al., 2024) accepts sparse or dense trajectories, and Time-to-Move (Singer et al., 2025) guides a frozen generator with coarse animations. 3DTrajMaster (Fu et al., 2024) specifies entity-level 6DoF trajectories; MotionCanvas (Xing et al., 2025) maps scene-aware camera and object controls to screen-space conditions.

Joint camera and object control in 3D.

SymphoMotion (Zhang et al., 2026a) combines geometry-aware camera guidance, 2D visual signals, and 3D trajectory embeddings; VerseCrafter (Zheng et al., 2026) renders background point clouds and object Gaussian trajectories into conditioning maps. FlexTraj (Zhang et al., 2026b) encodes persistent track and segmentation identities in control videos; Edit-by-Track (Lee et al., 2025) edits using paired source and target 3D tracks. Go-with-the-Track (Namekata et al., 2026) uses reference-anchored tracks for compositing, camera control, and object motion. MoRight (Liu et al., 2026) decouples camera and object motion via canonical static-view trajectories and cross-view attention. UniCaMo (Vu et al., 2026) constructs motion-consistent noise with occlusion-informed warping. In GenCine, artist-placed local 3D handles share the camera’s world frame. Mapping their persistent identities and current positions into conditioning maps jointly encodes camera and object motion.

3 Method

GenCine learns to generate a video from a reference image, a camera path, and local foreground trajectories. Training controls are recovered from videos; inference controls are supplied by the artist. Both pass through the same three steps (Fig. 3): (i) Place the controls in each view. Project background and handle points through the specified camera so the model knows where guidance applies. (ii) Preserve identity and 3D motion. Use fixed handle colors to identify regions across frames and separate XYZ maps to describe their positions relative to the static scene. (iii) Learn to follow the guidance. Encode the maps with the frozen video autoencoder and train adaptation modules on paired videos, reference images, and controls.

3.1 Scene Scaffold and Motion Authoring

Given an image 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}, we estimate depth 𝐃0\mathbf{D}_{0} using an off-the-shelf estimator (Huang et al., 2025) and take the initial camera frame as the world frame. We back-project each pixel 𝐮=(u,v)\mathbf{u}=(u,v) as 𝐩𝐮=𝐃0​(𝐮)​𝐊0−1​(u,v,1)⊤\mathbf{p}_{\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{D}_{0}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{K}_{0}^{-1}(u,v,1)^{\top}, where 𝐊0\mathbf{K}_{0} is the intrinsic matrix. The artist selects foreground regions in a 3D viewport and assigns each a trajectory. Each handle moves its selected points as a rigid group. For NN handles, let ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i} be the fixed point-index set of handle ii. Its world-space support at frame tt is

where 𝐩t,j\mathbf{p}_{t,j} is the point’s position under the authored motion. The artist also specifies camera intrinsics and world-to-camera poses {𝐊t,𝐑t,𝐭t}t=0T\{\mathbf{K}_{t},\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{t}_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T} in the same world frame. 3.2 Motion Representation: Correspondence Maps and Rigid Handles

The motion representation in GenCine follows two principles: explicit correspondence and local rigidity. The first is motivated by motion correspondence in human visual perception (Ullman, 1979; Dawson, 1991); the second allows a few local controls to approximate complex foreground deformation (Sumner et al., 2007; Sorkine & Alexa, 2007).

  • •

    Preserving identity and 3D position. We encode world-space XYZ coordinates as RGB values. Static background coordinates provide position and persistent identity. For moving foreground points, we separate current XYZ from fixed colors identifying handles across frames (Fig. 4).

  • •

    Rigid motion handles. Multiple independently controlled rigid handles approximate non-rigid motion—for example, moving a person’s hands while keeping the torso still. This provides local control without authoring a dense deformation field or requiring an object template, skeleton, or category-specific motion prior.

Background and foreground XYZ maps (𝐅tbg\mathbf{F}_{t}^{\mathrm{bg}}, 𝐅tfg\mathbf{F}_{t}^{\mathrm{fg}}).

We project background and motion-handle points into each frame:

𝐮t=π⁡(𝐊t​(𝐑t​𝐩t+𝐭t)),\mathbf{u}_{t}=\pi\!\left(\mathbf{K}_{t}(\mathbf{R}_{t}\mathbf{p}_{t}+\mathbf{t}_{t})\right), (2)

where π⁡((a,b,c)⊤)=(a/c,b/c)⊤\pi((a,b,c)^{\top})=(a/c,b/c)^{\top} denotes perspective division. Background points remain at 𝐩t=𝐩𝐮\mathbf{p}_{t}=\mathbf{p}_{\mathbf{u}}, while handle points 𝐩t∈ℋt,i\mathbf{p}_{t}\in\mathcal{H}_{t,i} follow their authored motion. We resolve visibility by depth and write the visible points into image maps, using 𝐮t\mathbf{u}_{t} as the image location and normalized world-space XYZ as the RGB value. These colors describe geometry, not the points’ appearance.

Both maps share a per-axis normalization fixed throughout the clip. Let 𝐩min\mathbf{p}_{\min} and 𝐩max\mathbf{p}_{\max} be the coordinate-wise extrema of the valid first-frame points after depth-outlier handling (supplementary Sec. D), with bounding-box center 𝐨=(𝐩max+𝐩min)/2\mathbf{o}=(\mathbf{p}_{\max}+\mathbf{p}_{\min})/2 and half-range 𝝈=(𝐩max−𝐩min)/2\bm{\sigma}=(\mathbf{p}_{\max}-\mathbf{p}_{\min})/2. We normalize world coordinates as

𝒩⁡(𝐩)=12​[𝐩−𝐨𝝈+𝟏],where ​𝟏=(1,1,1)⊤.\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p})=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{o}}{\bm{\sigma}}+\mathbf{1}\right],\qquad\text{where }\mathbf{1}=(1,1,1)^{\top}. (3)

For points within the bounding box, (𝐩−𝐨)/𝝈(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{o})/\bm{\sigma} lies in [−1,1]3[-1,1]^{3}, and the shift and scaling map it to [0,1]3[0,1]^{3}. The background and foreground RGB values are

𝐜tbg=𝒩⁡(𝐩𝐮),𝐜tfg=𝒩⁡(𝐩t),𝐩t∈ℋt,i.\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{bg}}=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p}_{\mathbf{u}}),\qquad\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{fg}}=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p}_{t}),\quad\mathbf{p}_{t}\in\mathcal{H}_{t,i}. (4)

A static background point keeps its world position and XYZ color as the camera moves; only its image location changes. The background map therefore indicates both where the point projects and which world point it represents. A foreground control point’s XYZ color changes as it moves through the world. Using the same (𝐨,𝝈)(\mathbf{o},\bm{\sigma}) for both maps expresses foreground and background positions in a common coordinate frame and scale.

Foreground identity maps (𝐅tid\mathbf{F}_{t}^{\mathrm{id}}).

The foreground XYZ map alone cannot establish persistent correspondence because a moving point changes its world position and encoded color. We therefore assign each handle a time-invariant identity and render it separately.

To represent each handle as a compact image region, we approximate ℋt,i\mathcal{H}_{t,i} by a 3D Gaussian 𝒢t,i=(𝝁t,i,𝚺t,i)\mathcal{G}_{t,i}=(\bm{\mu}_{t,i},\bm{\Sigma}_{t,i}), where 𝝁t,i\bm{\mu}_{t,i} and 𝚺t,i\bm{\Sigma}_{t,i} are the empirical mean and covariance of its points. Projection through Eq. 2 yields a 2D Gaussian with mean 𝝂t,i\bm{\nu}_{t,i} and covariance 𝚲t,i\bm{\Lambda}_{t,i}. Let Ωt,i\Omega_{t,i} denote its image-plane footprint.

When handle ii is created, we sample a color 𝐜i∈[0,1]3\mathbf{c}_{i}\in[0,1]^{3} and reuse it in every frame. Let αt,i​(𝐮t)∈[0,1]\alpha_{t,i}(\mathbf{u}_{t})\in[0,1] be the Gaussian weight, largest at the projected center and decreasing toward the boundary. Within the footprint, we render

𝐜tid=αt,i​(𝐮t)​𝐜i,𝐮t∈Ωt,i,\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{id}}=\alpha_{t,i}(\mathbf{u}_{t})\mathbf{c}_{i},\qquad\mathbf{u}_{t}\in\Omega_{t,i}, (5)

Pixels outside all handle footprints are zero. Where footprints overlap, depth ordering selects the visible handle. The foreground XYZ and identity maps share this footprint, validity mask, and visible handle. The fixed base color 𝐜i\mathbf{c}_{i} identifies the same handle across frames, while αt,i\alpha_{t,i} determines its spatial weight. This construction produces three guidance maps 𝐅tbg,𝐅tfg,𝐅tid∈ℝH×W×3\mathbf{F}_{t}^{\mathrm{bg}},\mathbf{F}_{t}^{\mathrm{fg}},\mathbf{F}_{t}^{\mathrm{id}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}, with invalid pixels set to zero.

In summary, the maps provide complementary correspondence and motion cues. The background XYZ map supplies a static world reference for camera motion. For the foreground, the identity map identifies the projected handle, but does not explicitly encode its world-space motion. The foreground XYZ map supplies the control points’ current world positions, allowing the model to interpret their motion relative to the background.

3.3 Architecture

We build GenCine on a pretrained Wan video diffusion model and freeze its VAE and base diffusion weights. We train only a lightweight side branch for geometric guidance, convolutional projections between branches, and LoRA adapters in the main branch.

The frozen VAE encodes all three guidance-map sequences. The main branch receives the noisy video latent, the reference-frame latent, and the encoded foreground identity sequence. The side branch receives all three encoded maps and binary masks marking valid background projections (𝐌bg\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{bg}}), projected handle pixels (𝐌fg\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{fg}}), and the first-frame dynamic region (𝐌dyn\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{dyn}}). It operates at half the main branch’s spatial resolution and injects features through zero-initialized residual projections. Supplementary Sec. E details mask processing, input layouts, and feature transfer.

During training, each guidance sequence describes the motion in its paired target video. We apply Wan’s flow-matching objective to the target video’s noised latents, conditioned on the reference frame, text, and guidance (supplementary Eq. 19). The VAE supplies the latent representation; the trainable diffusion adaptation modules learn how the controls relate to the observed video.

3.4 Sampling Motion Handles for Training

Training videos contain observed motion but no artist-authored handles. For real clips, we estimate depth and camera trajectories with ViPE (Huang et al., 2025) and obtain motion trajectories with CoWTracker (Lai et al., 2026). Taking the first frame as input, we use its dynamic mask to sample spatially separated handles from visible foreground points with valid geometry. Each handle groups nearby tracks within a scene-scaled 3D ball and follows their motion through the clip.

After filtering unreliable tracks and handles, we convert the accepted controls into foreground XYZ and identity maps. We vary the number and placement of handles across configurations to simulate partial artist control. Clips without valid foreground trajectories receive background-only conditioning. Supplementary Sec. F.1 provides the sampling and filtering details.

4 Experiments

Training Setup.

We build GenCine upon Wan2.1-Fun-V1.1-14B-Control (Wan et al., 2025). We only train a small set of adaptation modules to learn the proposed geometry guidance maps. The model is trained for approximately 2020k iterations on 44 H100 GPUs.

Datasets.

We train on 4545k video clips covering diverse camera and object motions. Approximately 55k clips come from synthetic datasets, including Dynamic Replica (Karaev et al., 2023) and PointOdyssey (Zheng et al., 2023), which provide ground-truth geometry and motion trajectories. The remaining clips come from real-world datasets, including SpatialVid-HQ (Wang et al., 2025b). For these clips, we estimate depth, camera poses, and dynamic masks using our geometry extraction pipeline and obtain motion trajectories with CoWTracker (Lai et al., 2026). All clips are processed and cropped to 480×832480\times 832 resolution. We generate the missing video captions with Qwen2.5-VL-72B (Bai et al., 2025) and encode them with umT5 (Chung et al., 2023).

Evaluation Setup.

We evaluate on 7575 examples from the DAVIS dataset and the SpatialVid test set, grouped by content into Camera Shooting and Object Interactions. Ground-truth videos and camera poses serve as references. We measure reference fidelity using full-frame PSNR and LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) and their foreground-region counterparts (R-PSNR and R-LPIPS). Following CameraCtrl (He et al., 2025a), we report camera rotation (Rot) and translation (Trans) errors. We assess video quality using the subject consistency, background consistency, and imaging quality metrics from VBench-I2V (Huang et al., 2024).

Baselines and Control Inputs.

We compare with Wan2.1 (Wan et al., 2025) and five controllable video generation methods. In our evaluation, ATI (Wang et al., 2025a), Wan-Move (Chu et al., 2025), and Go-with-the-Track (Namekata et al., 2026) receive dense 2D foreground and background trajectories extracted from ground-truth videos. VerseCrafter (Zheng et al., 2026) and SymphoMotion (Zhang et al., 2026a) provide camera control and coarse object-level motion control. GenCine uses sparse 3D motion handles and a target camera trajectory derived from the same reference motion. Dense ground-truth trajectories are unavailable when authoring new motion from a single image; a similar input asymmetry is discussed in concurrent work (Liu et al., 2026).

4.1 Main Results

Fig. 5 compares GenCine with three baselines on artist-authored examples. In Living room, GenCine moves the green tunnel with less distortion than Wan-Move and VerseCrafter. In Bus, GenCine coordinates the intended turn with camera pullback, while VerseCrafter largely retains the bus’s initial orientation. Robotic arm further illustrates motion dependencies between connected parts. Go-with-the-Track moves the gripper region but leaves most of the arm static, while VerseCrafter introduces extraneous boxes. GenCine follows the end-effector path while articulating the connected arm segments. This coordinated response suggests that GenCine can infer motion dependencies within an articulated structure, using sparse local guidance to generate motion beyond the directly controlled region.

In Tab. 1, GenCine achieves the lowest translation error and R-LPIPS in both categories, ranking second in rotation error behind Go-with-the-Track. On Camera Shooting, it leads PSNR (16.6416.64) and R-PSNR (17.1617.16), and ties Wan-Move and Go-with-the-Track for lowest LPIPS (0.360.36 at reported precision). On Object Interactions, it achieves the lowest LPIPS (0.350.35), with PSNR (16.5416.54) second to Go-with-the-Track (16.5916.59). Other methods retain complementary strengths. Go-with-the-Track leads subject consistency on Camera Shooting; on Object Interactions, VerseCrafter leads imaging quality, while Wan-Move leads R-PSNR and background consistency. GenCine’s clearest advantages are translation accuracy and foreground perceptual fidelity.

These results indicate effective camera and foreground control with sparse 3D motion handles and a camera trajectory. Additional comparison examples and video versions of these results are available on the project website.

4.2 Ablation Study

We ablate the background XYZ map 𝐅bg\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{bg}}, the foreground XYZ map 𝐅fg\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{fg}}, and the side-branch spatial downsampling factor ssides_{\mathrm{side}} in GenCine. The default retains all guidance maps with sside=2s_{\mathrm{side}}=2 (half the main branch’s spatial resolution). Quantitative variants share training data, backbone, and optimization settings, differing only in the indicated component. Tab. 2 reports results on Camera Shooting examples.

Removing 𝐅bg\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{bg}} degrades foreground reference fidelity: R-LPIPS increases from 0.1840.184 to 0.2350.235, and R-PSNR drops from 17.1617.16 to 16.2016.20. These results support using background correspondence as a reference for foreground control.

As a qualitative illustration, Fig. 6 shows the intended task of moving the boat while keeping the camera fixed. The foreground-only result exhibits unwanted background motion, while the result with full foreground and background XYZ guidance better preserves the static scene. The middle row additionally shows background XYZ guidance only. The saved camera exports differ between the foreground-only and full-guidance runs, which limits attribution to background guidance alone.

Removing 𝐅fg\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{fg}} increases R-LPIPS to 0.2230.223 and reduces R-PSNR to 15.2615.26. Despite the highest subject consistency (0.9120.912), this variant reconstructs foreground motion less faithfully. With all maps retained, sside=2s_{\mathrm{side}}=2 improves R-LPIPS from 0.1890.189 to 0.1840.184 relative to sside=1s_{\mathrm{side}}=1, while R-PSNR decreases slightly from 17.1717.17 to 17.1617.16. It also improves subject consistency (0.8970.897 to 0.9020.902), background consistency (0.9420.942 to 0.9440.944), and imaging quality (0.6860.686 to 0.6910.691).

Overall, the default configuration achieves the lowest R-LPIPS and the highest background consistency and imaging quality among the tested variants. Additional qualitative examples appear in Figs. 1, 7, and 8.

5 Discussion

We presented GenCine, a system for jointly authoring camera and object motion in a shared 3D world lifted from a single image. Its guidance maps encode static background coordinates, persistent foreground handle identities, and current world-space positions in a form compatible with pretrained video diffusion models. This representation makes the intended 3D motion explicit where image-space trajectories alone leave it ambiguous. Our results show that a few local handles can compose camera and foreground motion, including a piecewise-rigid approximation to articulated motion, through lightweight adaptation of a pretrained video generator.

The single-image scaffold leaves occluded regions unmodeled, requiring the generator to synthesize unseen surfaces under large viewpoint changes. Local rigid handles are better suited to articulated motion than to fracture, tearing, or fluid dynamics, and authoring many handles can become cumbersome for distributed deformation. Independently authored handles also impose no physical constraints or causal interactions between objects. Geometry completion, automatic handle placement, and learned interaction priors could extend the range of shots artists can compose.

We used generative AI only for language polishing in manuscript preparation. Qwen2.5-VL-72B generated missing training captions (Sec. 4). The authors take responsibility for all content.

Ethics Statement

Generated videos should be identified as synthetic to reduce misleading use, with privacy and applicable data and model licenses respected.

Reproducibility Statement

Sections 3 and 4 describe the method, datasets, training setup, and evaluation. The supplement provides implementation details (Secs. C–G).

This supplement begins with additional qualitative comparisons (Sec. A). It then reviews latent video diffusion (Sec. B) and details the scene scaffold (Sec. C), guidance maps (Sec. D), architecture (Sec. E), training (Sec. F), and inference (Sec. G). We conclude with failure cases and limitations (Sec. H).

Appendix A Additional Qualitative Comparisons

Ambiguity in image-space control.

Fig. 7 examines an edit that moves a teapot toward the camera while preserving its orientation in world space. Image-plane trajectories constrain projected motion but do not uniquely specify the underlying 3D transformation. In this example, Wan-Move produces geometrically inconsistent motion across the sampled frames. In GenCine, 3D handles specify the intended displacement in the canonical world frame, and the generated sequence better preserves the teapot’s orientation and scene geometry. This example illustrates the benefit of making the intended 3D motion explicit when different spatial motions can have similar image-plane projections.

Camera and object motion.

Fig. 8 compares outputs from ATI (Wang et al., 2025a), Wan-Move (Chu et al., 2025), and GenCine with ground-truth videos for the same foreground-control examples: hiking, camel, and dog sequences. Each scene shows ATI, Wan-Move, GenCine, and ground truth in row order, sampled at six aligned timesteps. The hiking and camel examples illustrate foreground displacement and changes in camera-relative appearance, while the dog sequence highlights articulated motion. GenCine follows the specified foreground motion while preserving coherent scene context across the sampled frames. In the dog example, its generated poses more closely match the reference poses than the baseline outputs. These results complement the reference-fidelity metrics in Tab. 1.

Appendix B Latent Video Diffusion Background

Video diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020; Blattmann et al., 2023; Wan et al., 2025) learn a noise-to-video generation process. Latent models reduce computation by operating in a compressed space produced by a pretrained video VAE (Rombach et al., 2022; Blattmann et al., 2023). The Wan backbone used by GenCine adopts a flow-matching objective in this space (Eq. 19).

Given an input video 𝐕∈ℝ(1+T)×H×W×3\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{(1+T)\times H\times W\times 3}, where 1+T1+T is the number of frames and H×WH\times W is the spatial resolution, the VAE encoder ℰ\mathcal{E} compresses the video temporally by a factor ftf_{t}, spatially by a factor fsf_{s}, and expands the channel dimension to CC:

𝐳=ℰ⁡(𝐕)∈ℝ(1+Tft)×Hfs×Wfs×C.\mathbf{z}=\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{V})\in\mathbb{R}^{\left(1+\frac{T}{f_{t}}\right)\times\frac{H}{f_{s}}\times\frac{W}{f_{s}}\times C}. (6)

The VAE decoder 𝒟\mathcal{D} reconstructs the video from the latent: 𝐕^=𝒟⁡(𝐳)\hat{\mathbf{V}}=\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}). For Wan2.1 (Wan et al., 2025), ft=4f_{t}=4, fs=8f_{s}=8, and C=16C=16.

We represent the three guidance maps as RGB sequences so that the same frozen VAE can encode them. Binary masks are processed separately (Sec. E). To retain the pretrained visual prior, we freeze the VAE and base diffusion weights and train only the side branch, inter-branch projections, and main-branch LoRA adapters.

Appendix C Scene Scaffold Details

Depth and camera estimation.

We estimate first-frame depth with ViPE (Huang et al., 2025) and use the initial camera frame as the world frame. The intrinsic matrix 𝐊0\mathbf{K}_{0} is taken from the depth pipeline’s estimate when not provided as input. Pixels with invalid depth are excluded from the initial point cloud. Geometry-supported filling of rasterized background holes is described separately in Sec. D.

Dynamic mask.

GroundingSAM2 predicts the first-frame dynamic mask 𝐌dyn∈{0,1}H×W\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{dyn}}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W}, where one marks potentially mobile foreground. This mask partitions the initial point cloud and supplies first-frame conditioning. For the conditioning sequence, we pad subsequent frames with ones; this padding is not a prediction of foreground occupancy in later frames.

Coordinate convention.

The initial camera frame is taken as the canonical world frame, with rotation 𝐑0=𝐈3\mathbf{R}_{0}=\mathbf{I}_{3} and translation 𝐭0=𝟎\mathbf{t}_{0}=\mathbf{0}. Subsequent camera poses are expressed as world-to-camera transforms. Per-frame intrinsics 𝐊t\mathbf{K}_{t} are constant in our experiments unless the artist explicitly authors a zoom; we expose intrinsics per-frame in the construction (Sec. 3.2 of the main paper) for generality.

Back-projection and point cloud.

Let Ω={0,…,W−1}×{0,…,H−1}\Omega=\{0,\ldots,W-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,H-1\} denote the image domain and Ωvalid⊆Ω\Omega_{\mathrm{valid}}\subseteq\Omega the pixels with valid depth. For 𝐮=(u,v)\mathbf{u}=(u,v), let 𝐮~=(u,v,1)⊤\widetilde{\mathbf{u}}=(u,v,1)^{\top} be its homogeneous coordinate. Given the first-frame depth map 𝐃0∈ℝH×W\mathbf{D}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}, back-projection gives

𝐩𝐮=𝐃0​(𝐮)​𝐊0−1​𝐮~=(x𝐮,y𝐮,z𝐮)⊤∈ℝ3.\mathbf{p}_{\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{D}_{0}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{K}_{0}^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf{u}}=(x_{\mathbf{u}},y_{\mathbf{u}},z_{\mathbf{u}})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. (7)

With the input RGB value 𝐜𝐮=(R𝐮,G𝐮,B𝐮)⊤\mathbf{c}_{\mathbf{u}}=(R_{\mathbf{u}},G_{\mathbf{u}},B_{\mathbf{u}})^{\top}, the colored point cloud is

𝐏={(𝐩𝐮,𝐜𝐮)|𝐮∈Ωvalid}.\mathbf{P}=\bigl\{(\mathbf{p}_{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{c}_{\mathbf{u}})\bigm|\mathbf{u}\in\Omega_{\mathrm{valid}}\bigr\}. (8)

The dynamic mask partitions 𝐏\mathbf{P} into the static background 𝐏bg\mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{bg}} and potentially mobile foreground 𝐏fg\mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{fg}}. Throughout the construction, 𝐮\mathbf{u} denotes a 2D pixel coordinate, 𝐩\mathbf{p} a 3D world-space point, and 𝐜\mathbf{c} an RGB vector.

Authored handle support.

Eq. 1 defines the point set ℋt,i\mathcal{H}_{t,i} using the fixed artist-selected indices ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i}. The selected points move as a rigid group under the handle’s authored motion. Independently moving handles provide a piecewise-rigid approximation to non-rigid motion, and additional handles allow finer local control.

Appendix D Guidance Map Construction Details

Shared coordinate normalization.

The background and foreground XYZ maps use 𝒩\mathcal{N} from Eq. 3, with shared parameters derived from the first-frame point cloud:

𝐜t\displaystyle\mathbf{c}_{t} =𝒩⁡(𝐩t),\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p}_{t}), (9)
𝐨\displaystyle\mathbf{o} =𝐩max+𝐩min2,𝝈=𝐩max−𝐩min2,\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbf{p}_{\max}+\mathbf{p}_{\min}}{2},\qquad\bm{\sigma}=\frac{\mathbf{p}_{\max}-\mathbf{p}_{\min}}{2},

where 𝐩t\mathbf{p}_{t} is a static world point for 𝐅bg\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{bg}} or a current handle point for 𝐅fg\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{fg}}, and 𝐜t\mathbf{c}_{t} is its encoded XYZ color as in Eq. 4. Before computing the first-frame extrema 𝐩min\mathbf{p}_{\min} and 𝐩max\mathbf{p}_{\max}, we pull points beyond the 9898th depth percentile back to that depth along their viewing rays. This prevents distant outliers from inflating 𝝈\bm{\sigma}. For an encoded point, the inverse affine map is 𝐩t=(2​𝐜t−𝟏)⊙𝝈+𝐨\mathbf{p}_{t}=(2\mathbf{c}_{t}-\mathbf{1})\odot\bm{\sigma}+\mathbf{o}, where ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication. We compute (𝐨,𝝈)(\mathbf{o},\bm{\sigma}) once per clip and use it for both XYZ maps in every frame. Points within this bounding box map to [0,1]3[0,1]^{3}; positions outside it can exceed this range. Invalid pixels are set to 𝟎\mathbf{0}. Clips with extreme 𝝈\bm{\sigma} are excluded from training.

Gaussian fitting for motion handles.

We approximate each transformed point set ℋt,i\mathcal{H}_{t,i} by a 3D Gaussian 𝒢t,i=(𝝁t,i,𝚺t,i)\mathcal{G}_{t,i}=(\bm{\mu}_{t,i},\bm{\Sigma}_{t,i}) with empirical mean and covariance:

𝝁t,i=1|ℋt,i|​∑𝐩∈ℋt,i𝐩,𝚺t,i=1|ℋt,i|​∑𝐩∈ℋt,i(𝐩−𝝁t,i)​(𝐩−𝝁t,i)⊤.\bm{\mu}_{t,i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}_{t,i}|}\sum_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{H}_{t,i}}\mathbf{p},\qquad\bm{\Sigma}_{t,i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}_{t,i}|}\sum_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{H}_{t,i}}(\mathbf{p}-\bm{\mu}_{t,i})(\mathbf{p}-\bm{\mu}_{t,i})^{\top}. (10)

Handles with fewer than five points are filtered out of the training set. We regularize the covariance with a positive diagonal floor to stabilize the fit.

Fixed identity colors.

When handle ii is created, we sample an identity color 𝐜i∈[0,1]3\mathbf{c}_{i}\in[0,1]^{3} and keep it fixed throughout the video. Projecting 𝒢t,i\mathcal{G}_{t,i} through Eq. 2 yields a 2D Gaussian with mean 𝝂t,i\bm{\nu}_{t,i}, covariance 𝚲t,i\bm{\Lambda}_{t,i}, and footprint Ωt,i\Omega_{t,i}. Within this footprint, the rendered value is αt,i​(𝐮t)​𝐜i\alpha_{t,i}(\mathbf{u}_{t})\mathbf{c}_{i} (Eq. 5), where αt,i∈[0,1]\alpha_{t,i}\in[0,1] is largest at the center and decreases toward the boundary. Pixels outside all footprints are zero, and depth ordering selects the visible handle where footprints overlap. The foreground XYZ and identity maps share the same projected footprint, foreground validity mask, and visible handle. Fig. 9 shows examples of all three guidance maps.

Validity masks.

Two pixel-wise validity masks accompany the three guidance maps. The background validity mask 𝐌bg\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{bg}} marks pixels with valid rasterized background geometry, including supported holes filled by the refinement below. The foreground validity mask 𝐌fg\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{fg}} marks pixels covered by a valid projected handle footprint and is shared by 𝐅fg\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{fg}} and 𝐅id\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{id}}. The first-frame dynamic mask 𝐌dyn\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{dyn}} provides a separate cue, with temporal padding as described in Sec. C. Invalid guidance-map pixels are zero; validity masks distinguish them from valid zero-valued encodings.

Occupancy refinement.

The background XYZ map is rasterized with a z-buffer and then morphologically refined. Closing only proposes hole pixels; a proposed hole becomes valid only when a local 3D Gaussian fitted to the surrounding valid surface yields a camera-ray intersection. Unsupported holes remain zero and invalid. This local refinement does not reconstruct surfaces occluded in the input image.

Appendix E Architecture Details

Backbone.

We use Wan2.1-Fun-V1.1-14B-Control (Wan et al., 2025) as the latent video diffusion backbone. The backbone consists of 40 DiT blocks operating on the video latent produced by Wan’s VAE. The VAE and base diffusion weights are frozen; only the side branch, inter-branch projections, and main-branch LoRA adapters are trained.

Side branch.

The side branch follows the design of Wan-VACE (Jiang et al., 2025). It consists of 8 transformer blocks whose weights are initialized by copying from selected blocks of the main branch. The side branch contains approximately one-fifth of the main branch’s parameter count.

The default side-branch spatial downsampling factor is sside=2s_{\mathrm{side}}=2: it operates at half the main branch’s spatial resolution on the latent grid, using one quarter as many spatial tokens. This choice reduces conditioning cost and is motivated by the sparsity of the foreground XYZ and identity maps. Tab. 2 compares it with sside=1s_{\mathrm{side}}=1.

Projection layers.

At the first side block, a Dirac-initialized strided Conv3d\mathrm{Conv3d} downsamples main-branch features and adds them to the encoded guidance features. Each side block emits features that a ConvTranspose3d\mathrm{ConvTranspose3d} projects back to the main branch’s resolution. At an injection block ℓ\ell, the update is

𝐱ℓ+1=Blockℓ​(𝐱ℓ,𝐲)+svace⋅𝐡ℓ,\mathbf{x}_{\ell+1}=\mathrm{Block}_{\ell}(\mathbf{x}_{\ell},\mathbf{y})+s_{\mathrm{vace}}\cdot\mathbf{h}_{\ell}, (11)

where 𝐲\mathbf{y} denotes Wan’s text and diffusion-time conditioning, 𝐡ℓ\mathbf{h}_{\ell} is the projected side-branch feature, and svaces_{\mathrm{vace}} is its scalar control strength. Output projections are zero-initialized, so the side branch initially contributes no residual. The main branch still receives the foreground identity sequence described below. Transposed-convolution output padding is determined from the requested main-branch grid to align feature dimensions across resolutions.

LoRA adaptation.

We additionally apply LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) to the main-branch attention and feed-forward layers (qq, kk, vv, oo, and both feed-forward projections), with rank r=64r=64. LoRA gives the main branch a small amount of capacity to adjust to the new conditioning distribution without disturbing the bulk of the pretrained weights.

Input channel layouts.

The main branch and side branch see different inputs.

Main branch. Let τ\tau denote diffusion time, distinct from video frame index tt. The main branch concatenates the noisy video latent 𝐳τ\mathbf{z}_{\tau} with the encoded foreground identity sequence. The reference-frame latent 𝐳ref=ℰ⁡(𝐱0)\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{ref}}=\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x}_{0}) enters as a fixed one-frame token prefix:

main input=[𝐳τ​‖ℰ⁡(𝐅id)‖​ 0],prefix=RefConv⁡(𝐳ref).\text{main input}=\left[\mathbf{z}_{\tau}\,\|\,\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{id}})\,\|\,\mathbf{0}\right],\qquad\text{prefix}=\mathrm{RefConv}(\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{ref}}). (12)

Here, 𝐅id\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{id}} denotes the full sequence of per-frame maps, and ∥\| denotes channel concatenation. The zero block pads the input to the Wan Control backbone’s 4848 channels.

Side branch. We reduce the binary masks to the VAE latent grid using max pooling, preserving small handle footprints during spatial and temporal reduction. Let 𝐌^\widehat{\mathbf{M}} denote a processed mask tensor. The side branch concatenates the VAE-encoded guidance maps with these masks:

side input=[\displaystyle\text{side input}=\bigl[ ℰ⁡(𝐅bg)​‖𝐌^bg‖​ℰ​(𝐅fg)​‖𝐌^dyn‖\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{bg}})\,\|\,\widehat{\mathbf{M}}^{\mathrm{bg}}\,\|\,\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{fg}})\,\|\,\widehat{\mathbf{M}}^{\mathrm{dyn}}\,\| (13)
ℰ(𝐅id)∥𝐌^fg].\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{id}})\,\|\,\widehat{\mathbf{M}}^{\mathrm{fg}}\bigr].

Each RGB guidance sequence contributes C=16C=16 VAE channels, and each processed mask contributes 44 channels in the input layout, for 16+4+16+4+16+4=6016+4+16+4+16+4=60 side-branch channels.

Text conditioning.

Text prompts are encoded by umT5 (Chung et al., 2023) into text embeddings. The embeddings are injected into both the main branch and the side branch through Wan’s standard text-conditioning interface; we make no modifications to the text pathway.

Appendix F Training Details

Data and adaptation.

As described in Sec. 4, we train on 4545k clips, including approximately 55k synthetic clips with ground-truth geometry and trajectories; real clips use estimated geometry and motion. Clips are processed at 480×832480\times 832 resolution. We train the adaptation modules for approximately 2020k iterations on 44 H100 GPUs.

F.1 Sampling Motion Handles for Training

For real clips, we estimate depth and camera trajectories with ViPE (Huang et al., 2025) and obtain motion trajectories with CoWTracker (Lai et al., 2026), as in the main paper. Synthetic clips supply ground-truth geometry and trajectories. In both cases, we express foreground trajectories {𝐩t,j}t=0T\{\mathbf{p}_{t,j}\}_{t=0}^{T} in the canonical world frame and sample controls from the observed motion. Let 𝒥fg\mathcal{J}^{\mathrm{fg}} contain trajectories that have a finite, visible first-frame position projecting inside 𝐌dyn\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{dyn}}. For each configuration, we sample the number of handles from a predefined range and select seed trajectories from 𝒥fg\mathcal{J}^{\mathrm{fg}}.

Let 𝐪0,i=𝐩0,ji\mathbf{q}_{0,i}=\mathbf{p}_{0,j_{i}} be the initial center of motion handle ii. We sample its radius relative to the scene scale ss:

r^i\displaystyle\widehat{r}_{i} ∼𝒰⁡(rmin,rmax),\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{U}(r_{\min},r_{\max}), (14)
ri\displaystyle r_{i} =s​r^i.\displaystyle=s\widehat{r}_{i}.

The initial support contains all foreground trajectories within this radius:

ℐ0,i={j∈𝒥fg|∥𝐩0,j−𝐪0,i∥2≤ri}.\mathcal{I}_{0,i}=\left\{j\in\mathcal{J}^{\mathrm{fg}}\;\middle|\;\lVert\mathbf{p}_{0,j}-\mathbf{q}_{0,i}\rVert_{2}\leq r_{i}\right\}. (15)

We reject a new center if it lies inside the support ball of an accepted motion handle. This encourages different motion handles to cover distinct object parts.

Artist-authored handles use the fixed support ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i} in Eq. 1 and move rigidly. Training handles instead follow observed local tracks, whose support ℐt,i\mathcal{I}_{t,i} may change as tracks become invalid or reappear. Thus, sampled training regions need not be exactly rigid. We update each handle independently. At frame t≥1t\geq 1, we collect valid trajectories near the previous center 𝐪t−1,i\mathbf{q}_{t-1,i} into a candidate set 𝒞t,i\mathcal{C}_{t,i}. We fit an empirical mean 𝝁t,i\bm{\mu}_{t,i} and a regularized covariance 𝚺t,i\bm{\Sigma}_{t,i} to these candidates. For each j∈𝒞t,ij\in\mathcal{C}_{t,i}, the squared Mahalanobis distance is

dt,i2​(j)=(𝐩t,j−𝝁t,i)⊤​(𝚺t,i+ϵ​𝐈)−1​(𝐩t,j−𝝁t,i).d_{t,i}^{2}(j)=(\mathbf{p}_{t,j}-\bm{\mu}_{t,i})^{\top}(\bm{\Sigma}_{t,i}+\epsilon\mathbf{I})^{-1}(\mathbf{p}_{t,j}-\bm{\mu}_{t,i}). (16)

The refined support is ℐt,i={j∈𝒞t,i∣dt,i2​(j)≤τM}\mathcal{I}_{t,i}=\{j\in\mathcal{C}_{t,i}\mid d_{t,i}^{2}(j)\leq\tau_{\mathrm{M}}\}. If the seed trajectory remains in this set, its position defines 𝐪t,i\mathbf{q}_{t,i}. Otherwise, when the refined support is nonempty, we use its mean position. We then refresh the candidate set around the updated center, allowing a temporarily missing trajectory to rejoin the motion handle in a later frame.

A frame is valid when |ℐt,i|≥nmin|\mathcal{I}_{t,i}|\geq n_{\min}. Otherwise, it contributes a temporal gap. Let 𝒱i={t∣|ℐt,i|≥nmin}\mathcal{V}_{i}=\{t\mid|\mathcal{I}_{t,i}|\geq n_{\min}\} denote the valid frames. We retain a motion handle only when its valid-frame ratio satisfies

|𝒱i|T+1≥ρmin.\frac{|\mathcal{V}_{i}|}{T+1}\geq\rho_{\min}. (17)

We also measure the mean normalized footprint area of the candidate handle,

Ai=1|𝒱i|​∑t∈𝒱i|Ωt,i|H​W,A_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{V}_{i}}\frac{|\Omega_{t,i}|}{HW}, (18)

and require Ai∈[Amin,Amax]A_{i}\in[A_{\min},A_{\max}]. This removes motion handles that are too small to be reliable or too large to represent local control. We resample highly overlapping motion handles until the desired number of distinct supports is obtained.

For every valid frame, we construct ℋt,i={𝐩t,j∣j∈ℐt,i}\mathcal{H}_{t,i}=\{\mathbf{p}_{t,j}\mid j\in\mathcal{I}_{t,i}\} and rasterize it using the procedure in Sec. D. Invalid frames remain empty. We sample several handle configurations from each clip to vary the amount and location of foreground guidance. If 𝒥fg\mathcal{J}^{\mathrm{fg}} is empty, the foreground XYZ and identity maps and their shared validity mask are zero, leaving background XYZ guidance.

Training objective.

We adopt the flow-matching objective used by Wan:

minϕ⁡𝔼(𝐳,g),τ​[ℒFM​(𝐳,τ,c⁡(g),ϕ)],\min_{\phi}\;\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{z},g),\tau}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\mathbf{z},\tau;c(g),\phi)\right], (19)

where 𝐳\mathbf{z} is the clean video latent from Eq. 6, gg is the precomputed geometry context, c⁡(g)c(g) is its conditioning tensor, and τ\tau is diffusion time. Reference-frame and text conditioning are omitted from the notation for brevity. The parameters ϕ\phi comprise the side branch, inter-branch projections, and main-branch LoRA adapters; all other parameters are frozen.

Appendix G Inference Details

Artist interface.

The artist loads a single image into the Blender interface for GenCine. The system constructs the scene scaffold once from estimated depth, camera intrinsics, and the dynamic mask. In the 3D viewport, the artist selects foreground regions as motion handles and authors their trajectories together with a camera path using keyframes or drawn paths. Both controls use the same canonical world frame.

Partial guidance.

Sampling multiple handle configurations during training (Sec. F.1) exposes the model to different amounts of foreground guidance. With no foreground handles, 𝐅fg\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{fg}}, 𝐅id\mathbf{F}^{\mathrm{id}}, and 𝐌fg\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{fg}} are zero. The model still receives the reference image, text, and background XYZ guidance under the chosen camera path; foreground motion is left to its learned prior. When no camera motion is authored, the camera remains at its initial pose.

Appendix H Failure Cases and Limitations

Depth failure and occlusion.

Monocular depth estimation can fail on reflective or transparent surfaces and thin structures. Errors in the lifted point cloud propagate to the background XYZ map and can cause geometric inconsistencies during viewpoint changes. Even with accurate visible geometry, the single-image scaffold leaves occluded surfaces unmodeled; the generator must synthesize them as they become visible.

Piecewise-rigid approximation limits.

Each authored handle moves its selected points as a rigid group. Multiple handles can approximate articulated motion, but fracture, tearing, and fluid dynamics remain difficult. More handles allow finer control at the cost of additional authoring effort. Independently authored handles impose neither physical constraints nor causal interactions between objects, as discussed in Sec. 5.

Motion beyond the normalized range.

Both XYZ maps use the first-frame scene bounding box (Eq. 9). Points within this box map to [0,1]3[0,1]^{3}, but a handle driven outside it can produce foreground XYZ values outside this range. Authoring within the scene extent keeps the guidance values in the RGB range; we expose the per-axis scale to the artist in the UI as a visual cue.
